qa.name: Pectoralis Major
qa.origin: Clavicular head: anterior surface of medial half of clavicle. Sternocostal head: anterior surface of sternum, costal cartilages of ribs 1–6, and aponeurosis of external oblique
qa.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus; fibers twist so clavicular head inserts inferiorly and sternocostal head inserts superiorly
qa.innervation: Medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1)
qa.function: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; clavicular head flexes the humerus; sternocostal head extends the flexed humerus. With arm fixed: elevates the thorax during forced inspiration
qa.opposing_muscle: Posterior deltoid and infraspinatus (for lateral rotation); middle deltoid (for abduction)
qa.blood_supply: Pectoral branch of thoracoacromial artery; lateral thoracic artery
qa.clinical_note: Pectoralis Major has two heads with different innervations — the clavicular head is innervated by the lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C6) and the sternocostal head by both medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C6–T1). Its tendon twists 90° before insertion — the clavicular fibers end up inferior and sternocostal fibers superior at the humerus. Rupture typically occurs at the tendon during heavy bench press and presents with a visible deformity of the anterior axillary fold. The pectoralis major flap is a major workhorse in head and neck reconstructive surgery.

qa.name: Pectoralis Minor
qa.origin: Outer surfaces of ribs 3–5 near their costal cartilages
qa.insertion: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula
qa.function: Protracts and depresses the scapula; rotates the glenoid cavity inferiorly; elevates ribs 3–5 during forced inspiration when scapula is fixed
qa.opposing_muscle: Lower trapezius (elevates and upwardly rotates scapula)
qa.blood_supply: Pectoral branch of thoracoacromial artery; lateral thoracic artery
qa.clinical_note: Pectoralis Minor lies deep to pectoralis major and is an important surgical landmark — the brachial plexus and axillary vessels pass posterior to it. It divides the axillary artery into three parts (medial, posterior, and lateral to pectoralis minor). Pectoralis minor tightness is associated with anterior shoulder impingement and rounded shoulder posture. In axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, the muscle is often retracted or divided to access level II and III nodes.

qa.name: Subclavius
qa.origin: Junction of the first rib and its costal cartilage
qa.insertion: Groove on the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle
qa.function: Depresses and anchors the clavicle; stabilises the sternoclavicular joint; acts as a protective buffer between the clavicle and subclavian vessels during a fracture
qa.clinical_note: Subclavius is a small muscle also covered in the Shoulder Girdle region. Its most important clinical role is protective — it cushions the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus from injury during a clavicle fracture. This is why neurovascular injury is relatively uncommon in isolated clavicle fractures despite the proximity of these structures. The nerve to subclavius (C5–C6) occasionally gives a branch to the phrenic nerve — an accessory phrenic nerve.

qa.name: Serratus Anterior
qa.origin: Outer surfaces of lateral parts of ribs 1–8 (sometimes rib 9) by saw-toothed digitations
qa.insertion: Anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula; lower digitations insert into the inferior angle
qa.function: Protracts (abducts) the scapula; holds the scapula against the thoracic wall; with trapezius forms a force couple for upward rotation of the scapula — essential for arm elevation above 90°
qa.clinical_note: Moore classifies Serratus Anterior in the pectoral region — it is an anterior thoracic muscle despite acting on the scapula. Long thoracic nerve injury (C5–C7) causes medial winging of the scapula — the inferior angle and medial border lift away from the thoracic wall, best seen when the patient pushes against a wall. Causes include axillary surgery, mastectomy, and backpack palsy (compression from heavy straps). Mnemonic: 'C5, 6, 7 — wings of heaven'. Note: also included in Back — Superficial for reference.
